notes: Housing benefit revision route after 2001 regime change; official-error point fails on appeal rights.

enrichment.short_title: Beltekian: housing benefit revision and official error after 2001 regime change

statutes_considered.title: Child Support, Pensions and Social Security Act 2000
Housing Benefit and Council Tax Benefit (Decisions and Appeals) Regulations 2001

key_facts: Westminster City Council refused Mr Beltekian housing benefit in February 2000; a Housing Benefit Review Board upheld the refusal in September 2000 on the basis of a contrived tenancy.
After transitional provisions took effect on 2 July 2001, Mr Beltekian pursued review and supersession routes concerning the board's decision but had left the property in July 2000.
The council refused a March 2002 request to revise its original decision for official error and refused supersession because it would not operate retrospectively.
On appeal Thomas LJ granted permission only on whether review power survived after 2 July 2001; counsel then relied on Regulation 4(2) official-error revision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a Social Security Commissioner on housing benefit review and supersession after the 2001 decisions regime.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Commissioner's direction for a tribunal rehearing was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: A refusal to revise a housing benefit decision for official error under Regulation 4(2) does not give rise to a right of appeal to a Social Security Appeal Tribunal because Schedule 7 paragraph 6 applies only to relevant decisions made or revised, not to refusals to revise.
legal_issues: Whether review of pre-2001 housing benefit decisions remained available after 2 July 2001
Whether Regulation 4(2) official-error revision could revive entitlement after the claimant left the premises
Whether an appeal lay against refusal to revise for official error
Whether the Commissioner should have directed a rehearing on Regulation 79(2) representations
index_terms: no appeal from refusal to revise

notes: Detailed sports disciplinary JR; apparent bias and Melville deliberation ground succeed.

enrichment.short_title: Flaherty v NGRC: quashing greyhound doping finding for bias and procedural unfairness
key_facts: Greyhound owner TF was fined £400 after NGRC Stewards found he administered a prohibited substance to Knockeevan King before a 2002 Greyhound Derby heat at Wimbledon.
TF challenged the finding for apparent bias of Steward Mr Critall, who had long acted as WGS's retained vet and forcefully defended stadium security.
NGRC senior official Mr Melville remained present during the Stewards' private deliberations after the hearing closed.
TF also complained about urine sampling procedure and other natural justice points.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court claim challenging a domestic disciplinary decision of NGRC Stewards under contract and public law.
enrichment.outcome: TF's challenge succeeded on apparent bias of Mr Critall and on Mr Melville's presence during deliberations; the Stewards' decision was set aside.
enrichment.ratio: A fair-minded observer would conclude there was a real possibility of bias where a Steward had a long commercial relationship with the stadium whose security was in issue and had not fully disclosed it; separately, a senior official's presence during a tribunal's deliberations is procedural unfairness that cannot be cured by proof of no actual injustice.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Critall was apparently biased and whether any waiver was effective
Whether Mr Melville's presence during Stewards' deliberations vitiated the inquiry
Whether NGRC urine sampling rules required split A and B samples
Extent of judicial supervision of sports governing bodies

notes: Part 36.21 matching-offer costs ruling with Petrotrade spirit applied.

enrichment.short_title: Read v Edmed: indemnity costs when Part 36 liability offer matched exactly
key_facts: Mrs Read, aged 80, was knocked off her bicycle in November 2000 and issued personal injury proceedings in November 2003.
Before issue she offered under Part 36 to accept 50:50 liability plus costs; the defendant's insurers declined on 19 August 2003.
On a preliminary liability trial in November 2004 the judge found equal contributory negligence and 50% recovery.
The claimant sought indemnity costs and enhanced interest under CPR 36.21 from expiry of the offer.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further hearing on costs after preliminary issue trial on liability in a Queen's Bench personal injury claim.
enrichment.outcome: CPR 36.21 held not to apply where the judgment matched but did not beat the offer; the court exercised discretion to award standard costs to 18 August 2003 and indemnity costs thereafter with 6% interest on indemnity costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where CPR 36.21(1) does not apply because the judgment is no more advantageous than the claimant's Part 36 offer, the court may still award indemnity costs from expiry of a valid pre-action Part 36 offer under its general costs discretion and the spirit of rule 36.21 when the defendant is no better off than if the offer had been accepted.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 36.21 applies when the court's apportionment exactly matches the claimant's Part 36 offer
Whether indemnity costs and interest can be awarded outside the literal wording of 36.21
Application of Petrotrade and McPhilemy to proportionate liability offers
Whether tactical sub-threshold offers are required to trigger Part 36 consequences

McPhilemy v Times Newspapers Ltd (No 2) [2002] 1 WLR 934
Huck v Robson [2002] EWCA Civ 398
Pitalis v Sherafetin [1986] 1 QB 868

notes: Post-mediation TCC dilapidations trial; roof and fees claims dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Riverside v Blackhawk: industrial lease roof dilapidations claim dismissed
key_facts: Riverside claimed about £87,522 for full roof replacement and £36,211 for professional fees after Blackhawk surrendered a lease of an Ashford industrial unit in September 2002.
Most dilapidation items were compromised at mediation; the dispute centred on whether the asbestos cement roof was out of repair at surrender.
Blackhawk had carried out extensive roof repairs immediately before surrender; Riverside replaced the entire roof in late 2002.
Riverside's schedule of costs largely related to pre-surrender enforcement steps rather than a valid schedule of dilapidations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of remaining dilapidations claims after mediation of a landlord's damages action.
enrichment.outcome: Riverside's roof replacement claim dismissed in full; the fees schedule claim dismissed because allowed items had effectively been paid before issue; judgment for Blackhawk.
enrichment.ratio: A landlord could not recover the cost of wholesale roof replacement where expert and factual evidence showed the roof was in proper repair at lease surrender after the tenant's works; recoverable professional costs must relate to a schedule of dilapidations or enforcement of repairing covenants under ordinary dilapidations principles.
legal_issues: Condition of the roof at lease surrender on 28 September 2002
Whether full replacement rather than repair was justified
Recoverability of surveyors' and solicitors' fees under lease covenants
Application of Tate & Lyle principles to schedules of costs

notes: Registered social landlord transfer JR; Article 1 Protocol and procedural fairness grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Clays Lane Co-op: challenge to compulsory transfer to Peabody dismissed
key_facts: Clays Lane Housing Co-operative, a Stratford registered social landlord, was mismanaged and the Housing Corporation directed transfer of its housing stock.
The Corporation chose Peabody Trust over a voluntary merger with Scottish cooperative Tenants First, citing financial certainty and regulatory concerns.
CLHC challenged the transfer direction and Secretary of State consent by judicial review on Article 1 Protocol, Article 11, procedural fairness and Peabody's finances.
Keith J granted permission but dismissed the claim; the Court of Appeal refused permission on Article 11 but heard the remaining grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of permission to appeal against dismissal of judicial review of a Housing Corporation statutory transfer direction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all grounds heard.
enrichment.ratio: Where mismanagement justified a compulsory transfer, choosing between transferees required a compelling public interest balancing exercise rather than the least intrusive option test of Samaroo; procedural fairness did not require a meeting on cross-border dual regulation, and officers' green traffic-light assessment of Peabody did not vitiate the July 2003 decision.
legal_issues: Test of proportionality under Article 1 of the First Protocol for deprivation of property
Whether dual cross-border regulation concerns required further consultation
Whether undisclosed officer concerns about Peabody's finances amounted to mistake of fact
Comparison of statutory transfer to Peabody with voluntary transfer of engagements to TFHC

notes: Novel post-settlement press access application under CPR 5.4(5)(b).

enrichment.short_title: Guardian v Alvis: press access to settled trial documents under CPR 5.4
key_facts: Chan v Alvis, a commission dispute over military vehicle sales, settled by Tomlin order after an eight-day trial adjournment.
The Guardian sought copies of pleadings and Alvis witness statements from the court file for a journalistic story identified in the claimant's skeleton.
Alvis opposed disclosure; Chan was neutral. Rule 32.13 did not apply after trial ended.
The newspaper relied on CPR 5.4(5)(b) and open justice principles.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by a non-party newspaper for access to documents on the court file after settlement of underlying proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted for particulars of claim, defence, reply and listed witness statements; Alvis ordered to pay The Guardian's costs on the standard basis.
enrichment.ratio: The High Court retains jurisdiction under CPR 5.4(5)(b) after proceedings end to permit a non-party serious newspaper access to documents on the court file that formed part of open trial proceedings, especially witness statements standing as evidence in chief, where open justice outweighs general confidentiality objections unsupported by specific harm.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 5.4(5)(b) applies after proceedings have settled
Whether witness statements confirmed at trial are within the public domain
Relevance of the press's actual newsgathering motive
Whether Alvis would suffer specific damage from publication

notes: Retrial conviction appeal; recent complaint and Dr Aziz re-examination grounds rejected.

enrichment.short_title: R v Francis: retrial rape conviction appeal dismissed

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: The appellant was convicted at retrial of six counts of raping his stepdaughter J between 1995 and 1998 after an earlier conviction was quashed in December 2002.
J complained to her sister and carer Lorna in late 1998; medical evidence was disputed between Dr West and Dr Aziz on pre-puberty penetration.
Defence counsel deliberately did not lead Dr Aziz's penis measurement evidence in chief; the judge refused re-examination.
No standard recent complaint direction was given on Lorna's evidence of J's November 1998 disclosure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the single judge after a retrial at the Central Criminal Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal against conviction dismissed; renewed application for leave to appeal against the 12-year sentence also dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to particularise counts under Rackham was not prejudicial where the prosecution case was not confined to isolated incidents; exclusion of Dr Aziz's measurements in re-examination did not render convictions unsafe where the jury had her opinion on penetration, and absent a standard recent complaint direction was immaterial where the defence relied on the complaint evidence to show inconsistency.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have required further particularisation after the prosecution case
Admissibility in re-examination of Dr Aziz's penis measurement evidence
Need for a recent complaint direction on Lorna's evidence
Sufficiency of evidence and fairness of summing-up

notes: Pension scheme buy-out contribution construction in proof of debt and negligence actions.

enrichment.short_title: Kenrick pension scheme: buy-out contribution power after termination notice
key_facts: Kenrick & Jefferson terminated its defined benefit pension scheme by notice effective 31 March 1998; the trustee later wound the scheme up in April 2003.
The trustee lodged a proof of debt for about £12.2m on a buy-out basis in the company's members' voluntary liquidation.
Liquidators rejected the buy-out proof; parallel negligence proceedings alleged Pinsent Curtis failed to advise on contribution powers.
The buy-out deficit had grown substantially during closed-scheme administration from an estimated £1.25m–£2.37m.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined Chancery hearing of proof-of-debt appeal and preliminary construction issues in trustee negligence proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Trustee had power before 31 March 1998 to demand appropriate lump-sum buy-out contributions under clause L.1.1, but not on or after 11 April 2003 once the scheme had been terminated and administered as a closed scheme.
enrichment.ratio: Clause L.1.1 permitted actuarially advised lump-sum buy-out contributions before termination, but once all employers terminated the scheme and it was administered as a closed scheme under J.2 employer contributions ceased and did not revive on a J.4 winding-up absent express provision.
legal_issues: Construction of clauses J.1, J.2, J.4 and L.1.1 of the 1997 trust deed
Whether buy-out deficits could be demanded after closed-scheme administration
Whether L.1.3 allowed the principal employer to crystallise liability
Relationship between contractual contribution powers and section 75 statutory debt

notes: Limitation preliminary issues; site establishment delay claim held statute-barred.

enrichment.short_title: Birse v McCormick: limitation on delay and disruption claim barred
key_facts: Birse sought about £810,000 from McCormick for additional site establishment costs under a 1995 building contract managed by Fluor.
Birse made a formal delay claim on 14 November 1996, excluded from a next-day changes settlement, and resubmitted a revised claim in April 1997.
Fluor did not respond fairly or promptly; the action was commenced in May 2003.
Preliminary issues addressed when causes of action accrued and whether a separate fair-assessment duty existed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: TCC trial of preliminary limitation issues ordered after applications to re-amend particulars of claim.
enrichment.outcome: Answers: Preliminary Issue 1 Yes; Issue 2 Yes (Fluor obliged fairly to assess); Issue 3 Yes — claims statute-barred, accrual about 9 December 1996.
enrichment.ratio: Under the contract Birse's cause of action for additional site establishment costs accrued when Fluor failed to respond to the November 1996 claim within a reasonable time; resubmitting the same claim in April 1997 did not create a fresh limitation period, and any implied duty to assess fairly accrued at the same time.
legal_issues: When Birse's contractual cause of action for site establishment costs accrued
Whether Fluor owed an implied duty fairly to assess claims
Whether April 1997 resubmission restarted limitation
Construction of Articles 8.3, 14 and 17 of the contract

notes: Sex offender alias and perverting justice; totality reduction on count 4.

enrichment.short_title: Spencer/Pike: reduced sentence for sex offender name notification breach
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty to failing to notify a change of name under section 91(1) of the 2003 Act and to perverting the course of justice.
He gave false names when arrested drunk in Worthing in May 2004 and again in Cambridge in July 2004 while subject to notification requirements.
He had more than 200 previous convictions including repeated failures to notify and indecent assault.
Cambridge Crown Court sentenced him to 18 months on count 2 and 9 months consecutive on count 4, totalling 27 months.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence referred directly to the full Court of Appeal Criminal Division.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the 9-month sentence on count 4 was reduced to 3 months consecutive, making a total of 21 months.
enrichment.ratio: Consecutive sentences were appropriate for separate notification and perverting justice offences given the appellant's history, but the 9-month term for giving a false name when drunk lacked the sophistication of identity creation and was excessive having regard to totality.
legal_issues: Appropriate reduction for guilty pleas
Whether consecutive sentences were justified
Application of totality where false names were given without elaborate identity creation
Sentencing for repeated breach of sex offender notification duties
